title: System Calls
summary: The syscall interface end to end: what it is, how it differs from a library call, and the exact mechanism from calling read() to getting your data back.

slides.markdown:
A **system call** is the only doorway a user-mode program has into kernel-mode services — opening a file, reading from the network, creating a process, all of it goes through this one interface, built on the trap mechanism from [User Mode vs Kernel Mode](user-mode-vs-kernel-mode).

This topic follows one call — `read()` — from the moment you type it in C to the moment your data arrives, and builds the vocabulary (syscall table, syscall number, `strace`) you need to reason about what any program is actually doing underneath.

A system call is a controlled request from a user-mode process asking the kernel to do something the process itself isn't allowed to do directly — touch hardware, manage memory mappings, create or signal another process. It's the API boundary between "your code" and "the OS."

Every OS exposes a fixed, numbered set of these — Linux has a few hundred, each identified by a **syscall number** rather than a name, because names are a C-library convenience layered on top (more on this next).

The defining property: a syscall is the *only* legitimate way to cross from user mode into kernel mode. There's no side door.

slides.sectionTitle: System call vs library call vs API — the layering
slides.markdown:
These three terms describe different layers of the same call, and confusing them is a very common interview stumble.

| Layer | Example | Runs where |
|---|---|---|
| API / language feature | `fopen()` in C, `open()` in Python | Entirely in user-space library code |
| Library call (libc) | `fread()` wraps buffering logic around `read()` | User space, may or may not syscall every time |
| System call | `read()` (syscall number 0 on x86-64) | Traps into the kernel |

A library call doesn't always mean a syscall happens: `fread()` from stdio often serves data straight from a userspace buffer without touching the kernel at all, only issuing the underlying `read()` syscall when that buffer runs dry.

**How to decide which layer you're looking at:** if it can be reimplemented purely in user-space code with no OS help, it's a library/API call; if the CPU must trap into kernel mode, it's a syscall.

slides.sectionTitle: Categories of syscalls: process, file, device, information, communication
slides.markdown:
Syscalls cluster into a handful of functional categories worth knowing by name. **Process control** — `fork`, `exec`, `exit`, `wait` — creates, replaces, and reaps processes. **File management** — `open`, `read`, `write`, `close` — operates on files and, on Unix, on the many things files pretend to be (pipes, devices, sockets).

**Device management** — `ioctl`, device-specific control calls — configures hardware behavior that doesn't fit the read/write model. **Information maintenance** — `getpid`, `time`, `uname` — asks the kernel about system or process state rather than acting on it. **Communication** — `pipe`, `socket`, `send`, `recv` — moves data between processes or across a network.

Recognizing the category tells you what to expect from a call before you even read its docs — a "device management" call is likely hardware-specific and non-portable, while "information maintenance" calls are cheap and side-effect-free.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: anatomy of a syscall — application to kernel and back
slides.markdown:
![read() syscall sequence through glibc and kernel](assets/syscall-sequence.svg)

The glibc layer matters here: your C code never issues the trap instruction directly, it calls a small glibc wrapper (`read()`) that packages the syscall number and arguments into the CPU registers the kernel's entry point expects, then executes the trap.

This is also why static-linking or `syscall()`-level languages can bypass glibc entirely — they hand-assemble the registers and issue the trap themselves, which is exactly what tools like `strace` intercept and print.

slides.sectionTitle: The syscall table and syscall numbers
slides.markdown:
Inside the kernel, the **syscall table** is essentially an array of function pointers indexed by syscall number: number 0 might map to `sys_read`, number 1 to `sys_write`, and so on (the exact numbers are architecture-specific and documented, e.g. in Linux's `unistd_64.h`). When a trap arrives, the kernel reads the number the caller placed in a specific register and jumps straight to `table[number]` — no name lookup, no string comparison, just an array index.

This is why syscall numbers, not names, are the actual ABI (application binary interface): a statically-linked binary compiled against one kernel version's syscall numbers can break if numbers ever shifted — which is precisely why the Linux syscall table is append-only and numbers are never reused or reordered once assigned.

Understanding this also explains sandboxing tools like `seccomp`: they filter directly on syscall number, whitelisting or blacklisting specific table entries a process is allowed to invoke.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: tracing a syscall with strace on a simple program
slides.markdown:
`strace` intercepts every syscall a process makes and prints its name, arguments, and return value — the fastest way to see what a program "really" does versus what its source suggests.

```bash
$ strace -e trace=open,read,write,close cat hello.txt
openat(AT_FDCWD, "hello.txt", O_RDONLY) = 3
read(3, "Hello, world!\n", 131072)     = 14
write(1, "Hello, world!\n", 14)        = 14
read(3, "", 131072)                   = 0
close(3)                              = 0
```

Even `cat`, one of the simplest Unix tools, reveals real detail here: it opens the file (`openat`, the modern replacement for `open`), reads in one chunk up to a 128KB buffer, writes that chunk to stdout (file descriptor 1), reads again to confirm end-of-file (return value 0 means EOF), then closes the file descriptor.

slides.sectionTitle: Common syscalls to know: fork, exec, wait, read, write, open, close, mmap
slides.markdown:
A short list every candidate should recognize instantly. `fork()` clones the calling process into a near-identical parent and child. `exec()` (family: `execve`, `execvp`) replaces the calling process's memory image with a new program, keeping the same PID. `wait()` blocks a parent until a child exits, reaping its exit status.

`open()`/`close()` acquire and release a file descriptor; `read()`/`write()` move bytes through it. `mmap()` maps a file or anonymous memory directly into a process's address space — it's how most modern loaders bring executable code into memory and how databases implement memory-mapped file access instead of explicit `read`/`write` loops.

The classic combination — `fork()` then `exec()` — is exactly how a shell launches every command you type: fork a child, then have that child exec the new program, while the parent shell calls `wait()` to know when it finishes.

**Wrong belief:** "Sending SIGKILL to a process is a system call the target process handles."

**Why it's wrong:** a **signal** is an asynchronous notification the kernel delivers *to* a process (interrupting its normal flow to run a handler, or in `SIGKILL`'s case, terminating it unconditionally with no handler possible). A **syscall** is a synchronous request a process makes *of* the kernel. `kill()` is the syscall — invoked by the sender to ask the kernel to deliver a signal — but the signal itself arrives on the receiving process asynchronously, at a kernel-chosen moment, not as that process's own syscall.

**Correct model:** syscalls are pull (you ask the kernel for something and block until it responds); signals are push (the kernel interrupts you when something happens, on its own schedule). `SIGKILL` specifically bypasses the target's own code entirely — it cannot be caught, blocked, or ignored, which is why it works even on unresponsive or deadlocked processes.

slides.sectionTitle: Senior nuance: vDSO and avoiding the trap entirely
slides.markdown:
Not every "syscall-shaped" call actually traps into the kernel. Linux's **vDSO** (virtual dynamic shared object) maps a small chunk of kernel-provided code directly into every process's address space for a handful of very frequent, read-only-ish calls — most notably `gettimeofday()`/`clock_gettime()`. Instead of a full mode switch, the call executes entirely in user mode, reading a memory page the kernel keeps updated.

This exists purely for performance: on a system doing millions of timestamp reads per second (metrics, tracing, logging), a real syscall for each one would dominate CPU time. Measuring the difference makes the point vivid — a vDSO-backed `clock_gettime()` call typically runs in tens of nanoseconds, versus several hundred nanoseconds to a microisecond for a true trap-based syscall.

The interview payoff: knowing vDSO exists shows you understand syscall cost is a real engineering constraint that kernel developers actively optimize around, not just an academic detail.

slides.sectionTitle: How this shows up in production
slides.markdown:
Production sandboxing is built directly on syscall filtering. Docker's default seccomp profile blocks roughly 40+ syscalls (including things like `reboot` and raw `mount`) that a containerized process almost never legitimately needs — because containers share the host kernel, restricting *which* syscalls a container can even attempt shrinks the kernel attack surface available to a compromised container.

Cloud functions (AWS Lambda, Cloud Run) push this further with gVisor-style user-space kernels that intercept syscalls in userspace and re-implement a safe subset themselves, trading some performance for much stronger isolation between tenants sharing physical hosts.

When you evaluate "how sandboxed is this runtime," the real question underneath is always the same one this topic covers: which syscalls can code inside it actually reach, and what intercepts them before the real kernel does.
